name: Victor Silva

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for doing this, Victor. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're independent, with no links to AI companies, employers, unions or political parties. Everything here is confidential, so you can tell me the public version and the private one. Can you start by telling me about a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Depends on the week. I'm on a transmission crew, so the big steel towers, the high-voltage lines that carry power between regions. Right now we're restringing a line across the plateau, so I'm living in a motel in a town with one petrol station, up at five, harness on by six-thirty, and sixty metres up a tower by eight. When we're not on a project, I'm back home doing maintenance on the shorter runs near the substation.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you down?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The view, honestly, and the problem-solving. I use AI every day for this job. I get it to explain old manuals, I check torque specs with it, I even ask it to build me a study plan for the next grade exam. What wears me down is the travel and the pay. My regional division pays less than the city ones, and I'm still paying off a loan for my mum's roof repair, so most months I've got a few hundred and that's it.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Are there other jobs like yours nearby?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Not at home. It's a farming town. If you want line work, it's this company or you go to the coast and pay coast rents. That's partly why I'm on the transmission crew, because the travel allowance helps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably post something like, told you the tech bros were overselling. But I'd also say the tools are still useful, because I use them every day. At work most of the guys would be pleased.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be a bit disappointed. I was hoping some of it would make the job safer, like drones doing the first look at a damaged tower so nobody has to climb a broken one. If it's all hype, we just keep doing it the risky way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going. I'd keep using the AI to study for my next grade, because that's a real raise, maybe fifteen percent. I'd try to get on the overtime projects to finish paying off the roof loan by next summer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Slightly let down, but calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned climbing broken towers. Has that happened to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Once, after an ice storm two winters ago. A leg on the tower was bent and we had to go up to put temporary stays on. I remember thinking, a drone could have looked at this for us and I could have stayed on the ground eating my sandwich.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do your colleagues use AI the way you do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really. A couple of the older guys call it my imaginary friend. But they ask me to check things with it all the time, so they come round.

S0.say: The tech companies oversold it, but the tools are still useful because he uses them every day. Most of his crew would be pleased.
S0.think: He'd be slightly disappointed, because he hoped drones and AI would make climbing damaged towers safer. If it's all hype, the risky way stays.
S0.do: Keeps working and keeps using AI to study for his next grade, worth about fifteen percent more pay. Takes overtime projects to clear his mother's roof loan by next summer.
S0.quote: I remember thinking, a drone could have looked at this for us and I could have stayed on the ground eating my sandwich.
S0.fieldNote: Victor is the rare lineworker who wants more technology, mainly for safety after climbing an ice-damaged tower. His thin cushion comes from family obligation, not spending. He's already the crew's informal AI helper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is good if it's done right, meaning workers get trained and the company shares the savings. I'd say it at work and online. I'd also say the union should be pushing to own the training, not just accept whatever the company picks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think it's good for me. Drones, robot arms for live-line work, smart sensors, all of it needs people who understand both the tower and the tech. That's me, or it could be. The risk is the company uses it to cut crews and only trains the ones it likes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Straight away I'd get my drone pilot licence. It costs about six hundred and I'd pay it off over a few months. I'd ask to join any pilot project the company runs with inspection drones or robot tools. And I'd talk to the union about a training fund, because not everyone on my crew can just teach themselves at night like I do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty calm. A bit excited, actually.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Six hundred is a lot with a thin cushion. What gives?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The motorbike trip I've been planning with my cousin. That was going to be in the spring. I'd rather have a licence that pays me back than a week of photos on the coast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on your crew would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Joaquim. He's forty-eight, brilliant on the tools, but he reads slowly and gets embarrassed. If the new stuff means written tests and apps, he'd fall behind and nobody would notice until it was too late. I'd want the union to make sure the training is hands-on, not just a screen.

S1.say: This is good if done right, with workers trained and savings shared. The union should push to shape the training, not just accept the company's choices.
S1.think: It's good for him, because drones, robot arms and sensors need people who know both towers and technology. The risk is the company cutting crews and only training favourites.
S1.do: Gets a drone pilot licence for about six hundred, paid over a few months, and asks to join any company pilot projects. Pushes the union for a training fund for colleagues who can't teach themselves.
S1.quote: I'd rather have a licence that pays me back than a week of photos on the coast.
S1.fieldNote: He sees this scenario as his opening, and would give up a planned trip to pay for a licence. His progressive streak shows in his concern for colleagues like Joaquim who'd struggle with screen-based training. He wants the union to shape change, not resist it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next one. This is AGI by 2028. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the power grid is public infrastructure, and if machines run it, the savings belong to the public, not to a few shareholders. I'd post a lot about that. I'd go to protests for a universal income or something like it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd ride the first wave. They'd need people to set up the robots, fix them, watch them, and I'd be one of the first to say yes. But that's a year, two at most. If AGI can do almost anything, it can do my robot job too, and then I'm thirty with no savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask to move onto the robot and drone teams the first week they formed. I'd cut back hard, no eating out on the road, cook in the motel. I'd vote and campaign for public ownership and a basic income. And I'd use every month on those robot teams to learn whatever skills look like they'd last.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Part of me is excited by it, which feels wrong, and the other part is doing the maths.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why does the excitement feel wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I know guys who'd lose everything. I'd be the one getting trained up while Joaquim gets a letter. It's strange to be the one guy on the crew who'd be first on the robot team and first to know it won't last.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do about your mum's loan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pay it off as fast as possible while I still had the travel allowance. Then she's safe at least. After that I'd probably move back in with her to cut rent, which she'd love and I'd survive.

S2.say: The grid is public infrastructure, so if machines run it the savings belong to the public, not shareholders. He'd post about it and protest for a basic income.
S2.think: He'd ride the first wave setting up and fixing robots, but that might last a year or two before AGI does that too, leaving him at thirty with no savings.
S2.do: Asks to join the robot and drone teams the first week they form, cooks in the motel instead of eating out and pays off his mother's loan fast. Campaigns and votes for public ownership and a basic income.
S2.feel: Anxious, with an excitement he feels guilty about.
S2.quote: It's strange to be the one guy on the crew who'd be first on the robot team and first to know it won't last.
S2.fieldNote: He's the most likely to move first, but also the clearest that moving first only buys time. The guilt about being the one chosen over older colleagues stood out. His politics get sharper as the timeline gets shorter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now AGI by 2031. The same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to set up a proper public plan, retraining and a share of the gains for everyone. I'd post about it and push the union to get serious, because five years goes fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think five years is good for me personally. I could get a robotics maintenance qualification and be the person keeping those machines running, which would last longer than climbing. Long term, I don't know, but it buys a few good years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd start an evening course in robotics and automation at the technical college, about two nights a week. I'd keep climbing to pay for it and save the extra from the travel allowance, maybe a hundred and fifty a month. I'd join the union's tech group and argue for a share of savings going to workers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but more curious than scared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the difference for you between two years and five?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years, I'm grabbing whatever's in front of me. Five years, I can actually choose. With five years I'd pick my next job instead of it picking me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the course be hard for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably the maths, I was never great at school. But I'd use AI to tutor me through it, like I do now for my grade exams. It's a patient teacher, it doesn't sigh at you.

S3.say: Five years is enough for a proper public plan with retraining and a share of gains for everyone. He'd push the union to get serious quickly.
S3.think: Five years suits him personally: a robotics maintenance qualification would outlast climbing. Long term he doesn't know, but it buys a few good years.
S3.do: Starts an evening robotics and automation course two nights a week, paid for by climbing, and saves about a hundred and fifty a month from the travel allowance. Joins the union's technology group to push for workers' share of savings.
S3.feel: Uneasy, but more curious than scared.
S3.quote: With five years I'd pick my next job instead of it picking me.
S3.fieldNote: The extra time lets him choose rather than grab. He plans to use AI as a maths tutor, which he already does for grade exams. Even here he keeps returning to how gains are shared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Last one, AGI by 2036. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is enough to do it right, so if workers still get left behind, that's a choice someone made. I'd say that loudly. I'd push the union and vote for whoever has a real plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years feels okay for me. I'd be thirty-seven, which is young enough to change direction twice. My worry is less about me and more about whether we end up with a few people owning all the machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd still do the robotics course, but I'd also start something on the side, maybe drone inspections for farms and solar fields near home, because I'd have the licence anyway. I'd keep climbing for the first five years and save. And I'd get involved politically, maybe even run for the union committee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but mostly about the country, not about me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me more about the side business.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Farmers near home have solar on their barns and big irrigation lines, and nobody checks them. A drone flight and a report, maybe a hundred a visit. If I could earn a bit on weekends flying a drone over my neighbours' barns, I'd finally have a cushion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Isn't that the same thing AGI could do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, eventually. But in the first few years, someone has to own the drone and turn up. By the time AGI is doing it, I want to have saved something and be on to the next thing.

S4.say: Ten years is enough to do it right, so if workers are still left behind it's someone's choice. He'd push the union and vote for a real plan.
S4.think: He'd be 37 at the end, young enough to change direction twice. His bigger worry is a few people ending up owning all the machines.
S4.do: Does the robotics course and starts a weekend drone inspection service for farms and solar fields near home, at about a hundred a visit. Keeps climbing and saving for five years and considers running for the union committee.
S4.feel: Uneasy, more for the country than for himself.
S4.quote: If I could earn a bit on weekends flying a drone over my neighbours' barns, I'd finally have a cushion.
S4.fieldNote: The longest timeline frees him to think beyond his own job, toward ownership of the machines. This is the first scenario where he plans a side business, and he's open that it's a stepping stone. He wants to finally build a cushion.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. Not because I couldn't adapt, but because adapting wouldn't last long enough to matter. What would help is a basic income or something like it, paid for by the companies using the machines, and public ownership of things like the grid. And free training, so it doesn't depend on whether you're the type who studies at night in a motel.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe how it feels to be the one who likes the tech. People assume I'm on the robots' side. I'm not on the robots' side, I'm on the side of whoever owns them having to share.

headlineQuote: I'm not on the robots' side, I'm on the side of whoever owns them having to share.
portrait: Victor is a 27-year-old transmission lineworker who spends weeks in motels restringing high-voltage lines, and he uses AI every day to study and check specs. His savings are thin because he's paying off a loan for his mother's roof, and his regional division pays less than the city ones. He welcomes AI Plateau and Steady Disruption with almost no fear, seeing drones and robots as a safer future and a chance for him. AGI by 2028 makes him anxious, because he'd be first onto the robot teams but knows that wouldn't last. Given more time, he'd retrain in robotics, start a drone side business and push hard for shared ownership.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because even if he adapted quickly, the new work wouldn't last long enough to matter.
whatWouldHelp: A basic income paid for by companies using the machines, public ownership of the grid, and free training that doesn't depend on studying at night.
